title: Master’s Thesis
text:
Master’s Thesis (2026)
Technologies
Python PyTorch pandas NumPy Git GitHub Linux Jupyter VSC HPC Statistics matplotlib
Repository
GitHub Repository



Pharmacogenomics (PGx) aims to understand how genetic variation influences drug response. A major challenge in the field is the interpretation of rare and novel variants, many of which lack experimental or clinical annotations.
Traditionally, PGx variant effect prediction has relied on specialized pharmacogenomic ensembles and domain-specific prediction frameworks. This thesis revisits that working assumption by evaluating whether zero-shot state-of-the-art protein models can achieve comparable or superior performance without explicit PGx-specific training.




Can modern protein language models predict pharmacogenomic variant effects in a zero-shot setting without pharmacogenomic-specific training?






Methods used:

BCa bootstrap confidence intervals
Permutation hypothesis testing
Multiplicity correction
Bootstrapped AUROC and PR metrics







 Top zero-shot models capture strong functional signals in key metabolizing enzymes, achieving peak Spearman correlations between \(\rho = 0.58\) and \(0.72\) on CYP2C9 and NUDT15



 In clinical star-allele benchmarks, zero-shot models (CPT-1, AlphaMissense, AIDO.Protein-RAG) achieved macro AUROCs up to 0.86, matching specialized PGx frameworks like APF2 and PharmGScore across multiple functional tasks.






Zero-shot protein models achieve moderate to strong correlations with experimental DMS measurements across multiple pharmacogenes.
AIDO.Protein-RAG, CPT-1, and AlphaMissense consistently rank among the best-performing predictors.
Several protein models match or outperform specialized PGx prediction frameworks on clinical variant classification tasks.






HPC Scale: Executed zero-shot inference for 12 large models (including 16B parameter transformers like AIDO.Protein-RAG) on NVIDIA H100 GPUs using the Flemish Supercomputer (VSC).
Workflow Automation: Orchestrated reproducible data pipelines using Bash, Python, Jupyter Notebooks, Conda, and SLURM workload management.












Figure
Description





Positional functional landscape of CYP2C9. Each cell shows the



experimentally measured effect of amino acid substitutions, and missing data are shown in gray. Colors represent functional classes derived from the DMS assay thresholds | |  | The heatmap displays AUROC values for each gene-model pair. Labels on the left track the variant distribution (normal and increased vs. decreased and no function) for each gene. | |  | ROC curves for classifying extreme CYP2C9 enzyme activity phenotypes using DMS activity thresholds (< 0.2 vs. > 0.8).|

title: Hi, I’m Reinout
text:
I like solving problems with data.
I recently graduated with a Master’s degree in Statistics & Data Science from UHasselt. My interests range from statistical modelling and machine learning to data visualization and bioinformatics. I enjoy exploring new ideas, building reproducible analyses, and turning complex results into something people can actually use.
This website contains some of the projects I’ve worked on, including interactive dashboards, machine learning research, and other data science projects.
One example is an interactive dashboard on air pollution that Sophie and I created for a data visualization course: https://dataviz-5zhh.onrender.com/
